name: Cherokee
variant: Western (Oklahoma) Cherokee of the Cherokee Nation and the United Keetoowah Band; the Eastern (Kituwah) dialect of North Carolina also exists and is not taught
script: Cherokee syllabary of Sequoyah (85 characters), with a romanised pronunciation line; left to right
basis: Grammar order: Joyner, Cherokee Language Lessons Volume 1 (2nd ed. 2016, Oklahoma / Otali dialect, built partly on Cherokee Nation classroom materials): syllabary, set expressions, numbers, 'sees' as whole forms, I / you pronouns, question endings, greetings, numbers to 100, question words and names, negation, colours, plural prefixes, Set A / Set B with 'see' and 'have', copula, 'want'. Topic order checked against the Duke Cherokee 101 schedule (2024). Neither is one of the Cherokee Nation / WCU / NSU / Holmes and Smith syllabuses: none of those gave a lesson list I could open.
src: Michael W. S. Joyner, Cherokee Language Lessons Volume 1, 2nd edition 2016 (PDF, cherokeelessons.com): read nearly in full (about 300,000 of 306,000 characters, via a summarising fetch tool); lesson topics 1-22, dialect section (Otali, Elati, Kituhwa), pronunciation-guide conventions (underdot short vowels, tone numbers 1-4, ɂ glottal stop, g/k and hl/tl pairs, unwritten h), and all syllabary and romanised words used in titles

Duke University, Tsalagi Gawonihisdi 101 syllabus, fall 2024 (PDF on iwl.virginia.edu): week-by-week topics (sounds; classroom basics; numbers; family; introductions; colours / clothing and plurals; liking, wanting, needing and negation; object categories; emotions; body parts; tenses; movement; senses and weather) and goals (first, second and third person word-sentences, present and command forms, about 40 verb roots); it names no dialect, speaks of the 'Kituwah language' and includes a field trip to Cherokee, NC

Native History Association, Cherokee Language Tutor, Lesson 1 Small Talk (romanised phrases only: Osiyo, Dtohitsu?, Osda, Gado detsadoa?, Hatlv hinela?, Gadogi hadia?, Usganoli hiwonihi, Tla yigoliga, Wado)
Patrick Del Percio, 'Greetings', DAILP (Northeastern University) teaching article: ᎣᏏᏲ osiyo, ᏙᎯᏧ tohitsu, nihina 'how about you?' and other greeting forms
University of Oklahoma Press page for Holmes and Smith, Beginning Cherokee: description only (teaches the Oklahoma dialect; North Carolina / Qualla is the other main dialect); no table of contents

Western Carolina University Cherokee course, Unit 0 page (2007): sounds of the language (vowels a e i o u v; consonants d t g k h l m n s w y ts and the glottal stop) and the titles of Unit 1 Meeting and Greeting and Unit 2 Classroom Language
Cherokee Nation online classes page (cherokee.gov): only that free online classes are taught by Ed Fields each spring and fall through learn.cherokee.org; no lesson list

Cherokee Nation Language Department, teaching materials page (cherokee.gov): lists We Are Learning Cherokee (textbook and audio by Cherokee Nation Education Services) only as a 41 MB zip download with no contents shown; not opened (the shell has no internet)

Cherokee Nation Language Department, 'Cherokee keyboards' page (cherokee.gov): Windows 10 has a Cherokee keyboard pre-installed; macOS has the Cherokee Nation layout installed by default (phonetic layout a download); iOS / iPadOS have a Cherokee keyboard and font that must be activated; Android needs a downloaded keyboard; Chromebook needs Google Input Tools

Apple, iOS and iPadOS feature availability page: Cherokee is listed for QuickType keyboard language support and autocorrection, and is NOT in the VoiceOver, Live Speech / Read & Speak or dictation language lists
Google Cloud Text-to-Speech voice list (first part of the page read): no Cherokee entry (the list goes from Catalan to Chinese)
Microsoft Azure Speech language-support page: Cherokee not in the speech-to-text or custom speech tables; the text-to-speech table did not render in the fetch, so Azure TTS is unconfirmed

Web searches (result titles only, pages not opened; cherokeelessons.org was blocked): cherokeelessons.com posts on community Cherokee TTS experiments (Tacotron2, IMS Toucan, espeak-ng); a Tennessee Tech news release on AI for the Cherokee language; Keyman Cherokee keyboard layouts
note: From the sources: the dialect facts; Joyner's lesson order for the grammar (fixed expressions and numbers before any prefix; 'see' learned first as whole forms, he / they before I / you; Set A and Set B only at his lesson 17, after colours and plural prefixes; negation, copula and 'want' after that); Duke's topic list (family, introductions, colours and clothing, like / want / need with negation, object categories, emotions, body, weather). Joyner is a learner-made course book, not an official Cherokee Nation syllabus. Tried and failed: the Cherokee Nation online class pages (no lesson list; the cherokeelessons.org class pages were blocked), We Are Learning Cherokee (listed only as a zip download), Holmes and Smith (publisher blurb only), WCU (unit titles 0-2 only). Not found or not attempted: See Say Write and NSU course syllabi (searches gave no syllabus). The lead may want to swap the basis if one of those becomes available. My own judgment: cutting Joyner's 22 TPR lessons and Duke's 15 weeks to 27 A1 lessons; splitting the syllabary into four lessons by consonant row (the row grouping is mine); moving the classroom survival phrases and introductions forward; the food, prices, time, places / directions, feelings / weather and animals lessons as placed. Beginner limits (my judgment, in line with both sources; the Set A / Set B labels for 'see' and 'want' and the prefix shapes below are my own analysis of Joyner's printed forms, and naming Set A already at chr-see-i-you, before Joyner does at his lesson 17, is my choice): set phrases and whole verb forms first; then only the singular I / you / he-she and plural they prefixes of Set A (tsi-, hi-, a-, ani- in 'see') and Set B (agw-, ts-, u-, una- in 'want'); no dual, no inclusive / exclusive 'we', no object-person combinations beyond fixed phrases, no full tense / evidential system (the copula lesson shows is / was only), and 'have' by object category (solid / living) as a taster. Romanisation: the main pronunciation line uses the everyday practical spelling found in Cherokee community materials (osiyo, wado, tohitsu, Tsalagi): vowels a e i o u and v (the nasal vowel, roughly 'uh' through the nose), ts for the sound Joyner writes j, gw for qu, hl / tl as heard; stops are written as heard, so ᏙᎯᏧ is tohitsu although its first sign is in the d-row: Cherokee g and d are unaspirated (this account of aspiration, the 85 / 86 character count, and the yi- prefix in negation are my own knowledge) (between English g / k and d / t), k and t are aspirated, and the syllabary does not keep them fully apart (the g-row and d-row signs cover both), so writers must give each word's established spelling and not derive it letter by letter. The main line does not mark vowel length, tone / pitch or the glottal stop, and neither does the syllabary (that the syllabary omits these is my own knowledge, not stated in a source I opened); a second, optional pronunciation detail follows Joyner and the Cherokee-English Dictionary tradition: underdot for short vowels, tone numbers 1-4 after the syllable, ɂ for the glottal stop. Romanisations in titles: osiyo, tohitsu, wado, osda, gado, hatlv, nihina, Tla yigoliga, Usganoli hiwonihi, Gado detsadoa?, Hatlv hinela? are as printed in DAILP / Native History Association; all others are Joyner's pronunciation strings with the tone numbers and underdots removed and j written ts (so they follow speech, e.g. agowhtiha, not a letter-by-letter reading of ᎠᎪᏩᏘᎭ). Every syllabary string in titles was copied from the Joyner PDF (or DAILP for ᏙᎯᏧ) as returned by a summarising fetch tool, not from my memory; writers must recheck each one against the PDF or the Cherokee-English Dictionary (Feeling 1975). Family, food, time, directions, prices, feelings and weather lessons are titled in English only because I saw no verified spellings for those words. Voice: no Cherokee voice can be used in the app. Google Cloud TTS has none; Apple lists no Cherokee for VoiceOver or spoken content (so no iOS / macOS device voice); Azure's TTS table could not be read but Cherokee is absent from its other speech tables and I know of no Azure Cherokee voice (own knowledge); Android was not checked. The only Cherokee TTS found are community / research experiments (cherokeelessons.com Tacotron2 / IMS Toucan models, a Tennessee Tech AI project; pages not opened), with no service or licence the app can use, so the course is text-only like Cebuano unless the lead commissions recordings from first-language speakers (strongly preferred) or licenses a model with the community's consent; chr-US is kept as the tag and the app must never fall back to an English voice reading the romanisation. Fonts and keyboards (Cherokee Nation keyboards page and Apple's feature list): iOS / iPadOS ship a Cherokee font and a Cherokee QuickType keyboard with autocorrection (to be switched on in settings); macOS has the Cherokee Nation layout by default; Windows 10 has a Cherokee keyboard pre-installed; Android needs a downloaded keyboard (the Cherokee Nation publishes an Android guide); Chromebook uses Google Input Tools. The Windows font names (Gadugi, Plantagenet Cherokee) and Android's Noto Sans Cherokee are my own knowledge, not checked; the app should bundle Noto Sans Cherokee as a fallback so the syllabary always renders. Respect: Cherokee is endangered, with first-language speakers mostly elders (my own knowledge); the course should present it as the living language of the Cherokee Nation, UKB and EBCI, not as a historical curiosity, and point learners to the Cherokee Nation's free classes. Before release, the finished course must be reviewed by a first-language speaker or a Cherokee Nation language programme (e.g. the Cherokee Nation Language Department), including every spelling, recording and cultural note. Script detail: 85 characters are in use; Sequoyah's original set had 86, and one has dropped out of use (my own knowledge). The syllabary is taught in four lessons by consonant row.
hardest: The syllabary: 85 signs for whole syllables, and it writes neither tone, vowel length nor the glottal stop
Tone / pitch and long vs short vowels, which change meaning but appear only in the pronunciation line
Polysynthetic verbs: one word is a whole sentence, and the person prefix changes with the verb's set (tsi- / a- in Set A, agw- / u- in Set B)
Verbs that depend on the object: 'have', 'see them' and plurals change by animate vs inanimate and solid vs living

stages.en: Sounds, the syllabary and first words
items: chr-sounds
Sounds: six vowels with nasal v, unaspirated g and d, the glottal stop, tone and long / short vowels; Western (Oklahoma) and Eastern Cherokee
chr-syllabary-1
Syllabary 1: one sign per syllable; the vowel column (a, e, i, o, u, v) and the g / k and h rows
chr-syllabary-2
Syllabary 2: the l, m, n and gw rows, with Ꮏ hna and Ꮐ nah
chr-syllabary-3
Syllabary 3: the s row with lone Ꮝ s, and the d / t and dl / tl rows
chr-syllabary-4
Syllabary 4: the ts, w and y rows; reading whole words and what the syllabary leaves unwritten
chr-greetings
Greetings: ᎣᏏᏲ osiyo, ᏙᎯᏧ? tohitsu?, ᏙᎯᏊ tohigwu, ᏩᏙ wado, ᏛᎬᎪᎯ dvgvgohi (I will see you again)
chr-first-words
First words: ᎥᎥ vv (yes), ᎥᏝ vtla / Ꮭ tla (no), ᎰᏩ howa (okay), ᎣᏍᏓ osda (good), ᏣᎳᎩ Tsalagi
chr-classroom
Survival phrases as whole sentences: Tla yigoliga (I don't understand), Usganoli hiwonihi (please speak slowly), Gadogi hadia? (what did you say?)
chr-numbers
Numbers 1-10: ᏌᏊ sagwu, ᏔᎵ tali, ᏦᎢ tsoi, ᏅᎩ nvhgi, ᎯᏍᎩ hisgi … ᏍᎪᎯ sgohi
chr-name
Introducing yourself: ᏓᏆᏙᎠ dagwadoa (I am called …), Gado detsadoa? (what is your name?), Hatlv hinela? (where do you live?)
chr-pronouns
ᎠᏴ ayv (I, we) and ᏂᎯ nihi (you), and nihina? (and you?)
chr-questions
Question words ᎦᏙ gado (what), ᎦᎪ gago (who), ᎭᏢ hatlv (where) and the yes / no ending -Ꮝ / -ᏍᎪ (-s / -sgo)
chr-family
Family: mother, father, brother, sister, grandparents as whole possessed words (my, your)
chr-numbers-big
Numbers to 100 and prices: ᏌᏚ sadu (11), tens, ᏍᎪᎯᏥᏆ sgohitsgwa (100); asking how much

stages.en: Verbs as whole words: Set A and Set B
items: chr-see-he
Verbs are sentences: ᎠᎪᏩᏘᎭ agowhtiha (he sees him / it) and ᎠᏂᎪᏩᏘᎭ anigowhtiha (they see him / it)
chr-see-i-you
Set A prefixes: ᏥᎪᏩᏘᎭ tsigowhtiha (I see him), ᎯᎪᏩᏘᎭ higowhtiha (you see him)
chr-colours
Colours and clothes: ᎩᎦᎨᎢ gigagei (red), ᎤᏁᎦ unega (white), ᎬᎿᎨᎢ gvhnagei (black)
chr-plurals
Plurals by prefix: ᎦᏍᎩᎶ gasgilo, ᏗᎦᏍᎩᎶ digasgilo (a table or chair / tables or chairs); ani- for people and animals
chr-want
Set B prefixes: ᎠᏆᏚᎵᎭ agwaduliha (I want it), ᏣᏚᎵᎭ tsaduliha (you want it), ᎤᏚᎵᎭ uduliha, ᎤᎾᏚᎵᎭ unaduliha
chr-negation
Saying 'not': Ꮭ tla with the yi- prefix (Tla yigoliga)
chr-have
'Have' depends on the thing: ᏣᎭ tsaha (you have it, solid), ᎤᎭ uha, ᎠᎩᎧᎭ agikaha (I have it, living)
chr-food
Food and drink: asking for and offering, with ᏚᏯ tuya (beans) and ᎠᏆᏚᎵᎭ agwaduliha (I want it)
chr-animals
Animals and counting living things: ᎠᏫ ahwi (deer), ᏙᏯ doya (beaver), ᏩᏯ wahya (wolf), ᎢᏯᏂ iyani
chr-copula
Is and was: ᎢᎩ igi and ᎨᏒᎩ gesvgi; now, earlier, every day
chr-time
Days, seasons, months and telling the time
chr-places
Places and directions: ᎭᏢ hatlv (where?), here and there, near and far
chr-feelings
Feelings, body and weather: I'm hungry, it hurts, it's cold
